title: The Hundred-Pair Wall
covers: what a percent means as per hundred, modeling percents on a 100-grid or tape diagram, scaling ratios to 100, and percents greater than 100%
cert: understanding percents as rates per 100, including percents greater than 100%

intro.caption: Lesson 4-1 — understand percent. Drop Day opens at noon, and the crew built a 100-pair wall to track every shoe. Three gates and a restock boss stand between them and opening.

balloons.t: One hundred cubbies on the wall. Every cubby is 1 percent of our drop.
One hundred shoes and not one bird-size sandal. Tragic.
Seven high-tops on this small rack! That's 7 percent!
Seven out of TEN, Ruben. Percent means per hundred, not per ten.

pages.caption: Ruben counted the shoes without checking the whole. A percent always compares the part to 100.

balloons.t: Count out of 100 on the big wall. Scale up on the small rack.
This crate holds 20 pairs total, and 9 are teal. How do we get a percent?
Build an equivalent ratio out of 100. Multiply both numbers by the same factor.
Whoa! 140 pairs showed up for a 100-pair wall! Nothing goes past 100 percent!
My calculator says 140 out of 100 is 140 percent. More than one whole drop.
Nice math, kids. Bet you can't lock down the final inventory before doors open.
Hye-jin's calculator is never wrong, Sly. Beat it.
One hundred forty percent stocked and ready to drop!

win.caption: Percent means per hundred. When the whole is not 100, scale both parts to 100 first — and when you have more than one whole, the percent goes past 100%.

gates.title: Gate 1 · Read the Wall
gates.prompt: Read the 100-pair wall first, then fix Ruben's count on the 10-pair rack.
hints: Conceptual: percent means per hundred. On a 100-grid, each square is 1%. On a smaller rack, scale the whole up to 100.
Procedural: for 7 out of 10, multiply both 7 and 10 by 10 so the whole becomes 100.

steps: Practice rack: 4 out of 10 pairs are white.
Multiply both terms by 10 to make the whole 100: 4 × 10 = 40 and 10 × 10 = 100.
worked.q: If 9 out of 10 pairs on a rack are red, what percent are red?

items.label: 38 out of 100 pairs are low-tops. Percent = (%)
items.aria: percent of the hundred pair wall that are low tops

fb.msg: 62 is the pairs still left on the wall, not the 38 low-tops.
0.38 is the decimal form. Out of 100, the percent is 38.

items.fbDefault: On a 100-pair wall, each pair is 1%. Count the 38 pairs out of 100.

items.q: Cole's small rack holds 10 pairs, and 7 are high-tops. Ruben says 7%. What is the real percent?

options.fb: That is Ruben's trap! The rack holds 10 pairs, not 100. Scale 7 out of 10 up to 100.
10 is the whole rack, not the percent of high-tops.
30% are NOT high-tops. 7 out of 10 scales to 70 out of 100.

gates.pass: 38% on the big wall and 70% on the small rack. Ruben quietly puts down his megaphone.

gates.title: Gate 2 · Scale the Crate
gates.prompt: When the whole is 20 or 25 instead of 100, build an equivalent ratio with 100 as the whole.
hints: Conceptual: an equivalent ratio keeps the same comparison while changing the whole to 100.
Procedural: ask what multiplies the whole to make 100, then multiply the part by that same number.

steps: Practice crate: 3 out of 25 pairs are blue.

items.label: 9 out of 20 pairs are teal. Percent = (%)
items.aria: percent of twenty pairs that are teal

fb.msg: 9 is the count out of 20, not out of 100. Multiply both terms by 5.
20 is the whole crate. Scale 9 out of 20 up to 100.
18 doubled 9, which only scales 20 up to 40. Multiply by 5 to reach 100.

items.q: On a shelf of 25 caps, 14 have Kicks's logo. Which equivalent ratio finds the percent?

options.fb: That keeps 14 without scaling 25 up to 100.
That doubled 14, which only scales 25 to 50. Multiply by 4 to reach 100.
25 is the whole shelf, not the logo caps.

gates.pass: 45% teal sneakers and 56% logo caps. The crate is logged.

gates.title: Gate 3 · Past 100%
gates.prompt: More sneakers arrived than the original 100-pair drop. Can a percent go past 100%?
hints: Conceptual: 100% is one whole. If you have more than one whole, the percent is greater than 100%.
Procedural: for 150%, think of 1 whole (100%) plus half of another whole (50%).

steps: More than one whole gives a percent over 100%.

items.q: The original drop was 100 pairs (100%). A restock brings the total to 140 pairs. Who is right?

options.t: Ruben: 100% is the limit, so it stays 100%
options.fb: 100% is just one whole drop. Having more than one whole goes over 100%.
40 is only the extra pairs, not the 140 pairs compared to 100.

items.label: The side-wall goal is 40 pairs. 150% of 40 pairs =
items.aria: one hundred fifty percent of forty pairs

fb.msg: 40 is 100% of the goal. 150% is one whole goal plus half of another.
20 is only the extra 50%. Add it to the 40-pair goal.
150 is the percent, not the number of pairs.

items.fbDefault: One whole is 40 pairs (100%), and half a whole is 20 pairs (50%). Add them.

gates.pass: 140% on the main wall and 60 pairs on the side wall. Sly steps back from the window.

gates.title: Boss Gate · Count the Drop
gates.prompt: Three final locks before the doors open. Watch the whole on every lock.
hints: Conceptual: check what the whole is first — 100 pairs, 50 pairs, or a goal you pass.
Procedural: scale parts to 100 for percents, and split percents over 100% into wholes plus extras.

steps: Practice lock: 3 out of 50 pairs are green.
Double both terms so 50 becomes 100: 3 × 2 = 6 and 50 × 2 = 100.

items.label: Lock 1 · 64 out of 100 pairs on the wall are black. Percent = (%)
items.aria: percent of one hundred pairs that are black

fb.msg: 36% is the rest of the wall, not the 64 black pairs.
0.64 is the decimal. Out of 100, the percent is 64.

items.fbDefault: The whole is already 100, so read the count directly as the percent.

items.label: Lock 2 · 21 out of 50 pairs on a rack are gold-trim. Percent = (%)
items.aria: percent of fifty pairs that are gold trim

fb.msg: 21 is out of 50, not out of 100. Multiply both terms by 2.
50 is the whole rack, not the percent.

items.q: Lock 3 · The shop's goal was 80 pairs, and they stocked 200% of the goal. How many pairs?

options.fb: 80 pairs is 100% of the goal. 200% is two whole goals.
200 is the percent, not the count of pairs.
40 pairs is 50% of 80, half the goal.

gates.pass: Click! All three locks pop open — 64%, 42%, and 160 pairs. Drop Day is live!

journal.heading: Lesson 4-1 — what the hundred-pair wall taught us
rows: Percent means out of 100. On a 100-pair wall, 38 pairs is 38%.
When the whole is not 100, make an equivalent ratio out of 100: 9 out of 20 = 45 out of 100 = 45%.
100% is one whole. More than one whole gives a percent over 100%, like 150% of 40 = 60.
Never call 7 out of 10 "7%." Check the whole before you name the percent.
journal.quote: "My calculator says 140% is real, and it never lies." — Hye-jin

teacher.suggested: Use during or after lesson 4-1 (Understand Percent) as one focused read. Whole-class on a projector, pairs on devices, or independent practice. Covers percents as rates per 100, scaling non-100 wholes to 100, and percents greater than 100%.
standards: Understand percent as a rate per 100; model percents and interpret percents greater than 100%
